items.title: Subordinates’ human-AI collaboration and leaders’ diverse responses: A dual-process perspective
items.abstract: Human-AI collaboration is increasingly initiated from the bottom up, as employees independently incorporate artificial intelligence into everyday work before organizations fully institutionalize its use. This makes leaders’ interpretations and responses especially consequential: leaders can legitimize, support, constrain, or even undermine subordinates’ human-AI collaboration. Yet existing research has largely adopted an actor-centered perspective and examined how collaboration affects employees themselves, leaving limited understanding of how leaders, as salient observers and decision makers, react to subordinates’ collaboration with AI. To address this issue, this research develops a leader-centered framework grounded in dual-system processing theory and examines why subordinates’ human-AI collaboration can elicit qualitatively different leader responses and how these responses shape the sustainability of collaboration over time. The central theoretical argument is that leaders process subordinates’ human-AI collaboration through two distinct but potentially coexisting routes. The first is a deliberative, “cold” processing route in which leaders engage in relatively effortful causal reasoning and future-oriented evaluation. The second is an automatic, “hot” processing route in which collaboration activates intuitive threat perceptions and affective reactions. By integrating these two routes, this study moves beyond explanations that assume leaders respond to AI-enabled employees in a uniformly favorable or unfavorable manner. Instead, it proposes that the same collaborative behavior can generate constructive developmental responses, constructive change-oriented responses, or destructive retaliatory responses depending on the psychological process activated. Study 1 investigates the cold-processing route through two complementary mechanisms. Study 1a focuses on leaders’ causal attributions regarding why subordinates collaborate with AI. Leaders may interpret such collaboration as driven by performance-improvement motives or, alternatively, by impression-management motives. These contrasting attributions are expected to shape leaders’ willingness to invest in employees’ future development, including behaviors such as empowerment, developmental support, and promotion-oriented decisions. Study 1b shifts from motive attribution to future-oriented appraisal. Leaders may evaluate whether subordinates’ human-AI collaboration enhances the team’s future competitive position and adaptive capacity. When collaboration is viewed as strengthening the team’s long-term standing, leaders should be more likely to display change-oriented behaviors, such as supporting experimentation, innovation, and work-process transformation. Together, these studies show that leaders do not merely judge current performance; they also infer motives and anticipate longer-term consequences. Study 2 examines the hot-processing route by theorizing that AI-enabled subordinates can alter perceived status, influence, and control relationships between leaders and followers. When subordinates become more capable through AI, leaders may experience relative deprivation because their own comparative advantage or managerial influence appears diminished. This perceived loss can trigger a defensive stress reaction and motivate retaliatory incivility toward the collaborating employee. This mechanism extends current human-AI collaboration research by showing that leader resistance may arise not only from rational concerns about technology, accuracy, or governance, but also from self-relevant social comparison and affective threat. Study 3 integrates the constructive and destructive leader responses identified in the first two studies and adopts a dynamic perspective. Rather than treating human-AI collaboration as a one-shot behavior, it examines whether leaders’ responses reinforce or erode employees’ willingness and ability to sustain such collaboration over time. Development-oriented and change-oriented leader behaviors are expected to strengthen the continuity and adaptive quality of human-AI collaboration, whereas retaliatory incivility should undermine its sustainability. This longitudinal comparison directly addresses calls for research on the dynamic trajectory of human-AI collaboration and connects leaders’ immediate reactions to longer-term organizational digital transformation. This research offers three main contributions. First, it shifts the level of analysis from employees as AI users to leaders as observers, evaluators, and resource allocators, thereby identifying leadership as a critical social mechanism through which bottom-up AI use becomes either institutionalized or suppressed. Second, it introduces a dual-process explanation for leaders’ heterogeneous reactions, integrating rational attribution and future-oriented cognition with intuitive, threat-based affective processing within one framework. Third, it advances a dynamic view of human-AI collaboration by linking distinct leader responses to the long-term sustainability of employee collaboration with AI. Overall, the research explains not simply whether leaders support or resist human-AI collaboration, but why different responses emerge and which responses are more likely to enable organizations to convert employee-initiated AI use into sustained capability development and digital transformation.

items.title: Substitutive and Dialogic-Reflective Modes of Interaction with Generative AI in Education: Towards Preserving Learner Agency
items.abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into education raises the question of how cognitive activity is distributed between learners and technological systems. This conceptual paper distinguishes two modes of learner-AI interaction: substitutive and dialogicreflective. In the substitutive mode, GenAI performs cognitive operations whose development constitutes the intended learning goal. In the dialogic-reflective mode, AI-generated output serves as an external representation requiring the learner to compare alternatives, justify judgments, formulate or refine criteria, monitor understanding, and revise an initial position. The framework draws on research on cognitive offloading, scaffolding, self-explanation, cognitive engagement, metacognition, learner agency, and desirable difficulties. Particular attention is given to discrepancies between a learner's initial position and an AI-generated representation. The central hypothesis is that, under specific interaction conditions, such discrepancies may encourage learners to make previously implicit evaluative criteria explicit. Possible indicators for empirical testing include independent formulation, quality of self-explanation, contradiction detection, criterion formulation, confidence calibration, and transfer to a new task. The distribution of target cognitive operations between learner and system is proposed as a central variable of educational design.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

items.title: SwarmSafe-Delta: Isolating Message Effects on LLM Agent Safety
items.abstract: When a tool-using LLM agent team violates policy, aggregate outcomes do not reveal whether an upstream message changed the executor's action. We introduce SwarmSafe-Delta, a paired executable protocol that freezes upstream computation, varies real, hidden, and format-matched placebo delivery, and scores a single committed action against deterministic benign and risky policy states under preassigned budgets. Across four models and constructed optional tasks, real delivery at $N=4$ produces 21.4% risky-world violations, versus 5.0% with placebo and 1.0% with hidden delivery (paired differences +16.4 and +20.3 percentage points). Real delivery also improves benign task success, illustrating that suppressing communication sacrifices utility. In a second regime constructed to require an upstream lookup route, real delivery improves safe completion by 74.2 points relative to hidden delivery. These effects quantify message-delivery contrasts under specified information dependencies, not naturally occurring failure rates. Exploratory action-level analyses show that the effect depends strongly on whether the upstream message recommends a prerequisite check or direct execution; model differences also largely track these message compositions. The contribution is a controlled, execution-grounded measurement protocol rather than a general claim that agent communication is harmful or protective.

items.title: Swedish teachers’ perceived professional action competence in sustainability and climate change education
items.abstract: This study aims to explore how in-service school teachers in Sweden perceive their professional action competence (PAC) in Sustainability and Climate Change Education (SCCE). Drawing on data from an exploratory survey involving 202 primary and secondary school teachers in Sweden, the study examines three core dimensions of PAC in SCCE: professional knowledge, self-efficacy, and willingness to teach. Descriptive and frequency analyses were employed to identify teachers’ self-perceptions across these dimensions. The study reveals that teachers generally perceive their professional action competence in SCCE as well-prepared, particularly regarding content knowledge and teaching approaches, and they report high levels of intrinsic motivation for teaching SCCE. However, the results also show several areas across these dimensions in which teachers felt less prepared: (1) to facilitate collective action-taking by students, (2) to engage with community partners beyond school in the teaching and learning process, (3) to support students in dealing with difficult emotions, and (4) to assess students’ sustainability-related competences. The study provides valuable insights into the conditions that support or constrain the implementation of SCCE in schools and aims to inform the design of future professional development initiatives and contribute to ongoing efforts to strengthen teachers’ preparedness for transformative SCCE.

items.title: Sycophantic AI feedback and disconfirming evidence search among business students
items.abstract: Generative AI may influence learning by shaping which evidence students choose to encounter, even when it does not determine their final answer. This study examines whether sycophantic feedback is associated with reduced search for information opposing an initial business judgement and whether perceived judgement correctness accounts statistically for that relationship. A questionnaire-based decision task conducted in September 2025 yielded 405 retained behavioural records from students at 16 Chinese universities. Participants received one of two assigned feedback conditions and opened four of eight materials concerning a fictional business expansion decision. The sycophantic group allocated 36.7% of its openings to opposing materials, compared with 47.5% in the evidence-based comparison group, an unadjusted difference of − 10.9 percentage points (95% confidence interval − 15.5 to − 6.2). An exploratory conditional choice model that respected the four-of-eight constraint and adjusted for material preferences within initial positions yielded an opposition-related odds multiplier of 0.458 (95% confidence interval 0.326–0.645). In the common 297-participant path-analysis sample, under the principal ordinary-least-squares model, the estimated indirect component through post-feedback correctness was − 0.015 (bootstrap 95% confidence interval − 0.031 to − 0.002). This pathway was sensitive to school clustering and modest hypothetical residual confounding; the auxiliary self-report contrast was not significant. The findings locate a potential cost of affirming AI feedback at the evidence-acquisition stage. They support an account of altered information allocation more strongly than a uniquely identified psychological mechanism or a general decline in critical-thinking ability.

items.title: The experience-blocking effect of artificial intelligence assistance in emergency decision-making and response: Conceptualization, formation, and impact mechanisms
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can improve emergency decision-making and response without necessarily strengthening managers’ experience-based judgment. When AI takes over activities through which managers encounter situations, form judgments, and learn from consequences, current task performance may become decoupled from subsequent experiential growth. We introduce the AI experience-blocking effect (EBE) to explain this possibility. Across three interrelated studies, we develop an integrated framework linking substitutive AI use, EBE, experiential learning processes, and experience consolidation. We define EBE as a proximal, multidimensional task-process state comprising four formative dimensions: reduced exposure to raw situational cues, displacement of independent judgment generation, weakened ownership of consequences and feedback-based calibration, and superficial reflective transformation. Here, ownership of consequences concerns managers’ responsibility for relating action outcomes to their own prior judgments and expectations as part of learning. Reflective transformation involves reconstructing events, examining causes and counterfactuals, and deriving rules for future action. Each dimension captures a distinct activity, so the four dimensions are not interchangeable and need not vary together. EBE may occur even when AI advice is correct and existing skills remain intact: it concerns participation in activities needed to acquire experience, rather than judgment errors or skill decline. Subsequent learning changes and experience deficits are assessed separately. Adaptive structuration theory provides an account of how AI use configurations shape managers’ opportunities to participate in these activities. Experiential learning and naturalistic decision-making perspectives explain how such participation supports experience-based judgment, while organizational knowledge creation and team learning perspectives address how members’ experience becomes available to a team. These connections distinguish the organization of AI assistance from the task processes and learning through which its effects on experience may develop. Study 1 focuses on the conceptual boundaries and measurement of EBE. It combines critical incident interviews, exercise and debriefing materials, and expert assessments to define the four dimensions and develop a measurement instrument. Four reflective first-order dimensions form a second-order formative construct. Validation compares self-reports with task records and behavioral observations and tests whether EBE explains delayed experience outcomes after accounting for prior experience, cognitive offloading, AI reliance, and current task performance. Study 2 examines whether substitutive AI use increases EBE by manipulating the human-AI-task configuration. Supportive AI use presents original materials first and requires managers to submit initial judgments or reflections before receiving corresponding AI input. Substitutive AI use presents summaries, judgments, plans, or debriefing drafts first, placing managers in the role of reviewing preformed outputs. The study includes a no-AI baseline, maintains access to original materials, and holds AI output content and quality constant across AI conditions. Managers may still seek original information or challenge AI outputs under either configuration; EBE is therefore assessed from their actual task activities. Current task performance is examined as a parallel outcome for comparison. Study 3 examines two parallel, potentially correlated learning mechanisms in a longitudinal design using repeated high-fidelity simulations. Perceptual learning of situational cues involves learning to identify diagnostic cues and recognize situational patterns. Reduced cue exposure and displaced judgment generation may limit the searching, comparison, and integration through which these abilities develop. Associative learning of action-outcome relationships requires managers to connect their judgments and actions with subsequent consequences. Independently generated judgments and outcome expectations provide a basis for comparing anticipated and actual outcomes, explaining discrepancies, and revising action rules. When AI supplies judgments and interpretations before managers develop their own, opportunities for feedback-based calibration and reflective transformation may diminish. Repeated learning assessments and delayed tasks without AI test whether these constraints contribute to deficits in individual experience internalization. Novel scenarios and erroneous AI advice further test transfer and independent error correction. Team experience externalization depends on both what members learn and how they work with that experience together. Restricted individual learning may leave members with less experiential material to articulate, including diagnostic cues, judgment rationales, outcome explanations, and rules for future action. Sharing, co-construction, constructive disagreement, and collective reflection shape how this material is developed into shared experience. The study examines members’ experience records alongside team interactions, causal maps, and after-action reviews to trace this transformation. Team experience externalization is thus treated as a distinct outcome that cannot be inferred by simply aggregating individual EBE scores. By tracing how task experiences become resources for later judgment, this account extends the evaluation of AI-assisted emergency management beyond immediate task performance. It identifies where experience generation may be interrupted and how those interruptions may affect individual learning and team experience consolidation. Practical implications center on preserving original cue exposure, independent judgment, feedback-based calibration, and reflective transformation within human-AI collaboration, so that task effectiveness and the development of managers’ experience-based expertise can be evaluated together.

items.title: The influence of AI chatbots’ human-like and technical characteristics on users’ perceived addictiveness
items.abstract: With the widespread adoption of generative AI chatbots, their human-like and technical characteristics may enhance user experience while also increasing the risks of overdependence and potential addiction. However, how these two categories of characteristics jointly shape users’ perceived addictiveness remains insufficiently understood. Drawing on the Stimulus–Organism–Response (S–O–R) framework, this study developed a model integrating perceived empathy, social presence, perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, trust, emotional attachment, functional dependence, and perceived addictiveness. Data were collected from 345 Chinese AI chatbot users through an online survey and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. The results showed that perceived empathy, social presence, perceived usefulness, and perceived ease of use all positively influenced trust, which in turn strengthened emotional attachment and functional dependence. Both emotional attachment and functional dependence increased perceived addictiveness, with emotional attachment exerting the stronger effect. Mediation analysis further indicated that chatbot characteristics indirectly influenced perceived addictiveness through two parallel pathways: trust–emotional attachment and trust–functional dependence. These findings reveal the emotional and functional mechanisms underlying perceived AI chatbot addictiveness, extend the S–O–R framework, and provide implications for responsible design, calibrated trust, and dependence-risk governance.

items.title: The social embeddedness of trust in AI: Insights from AI decision aids in renewable energy siting
items.abstract: The rapidly expanding employment of AI decision aids in complex and controversial decision-making processes means that trust in AI is becoming ever more important. While existing research examines a range of human- and AI-related factors affecting trust, contextual influences are often only narrowly conceptualized as task characteristics or organizational settings. This paper argues that understanding trust in AI in contested decision-making contexts requires focusing on how stakeholders assess AI’s trustworthiness in relation to their prior experiences with decision-makers and institutions. We develop a framework that conceptualizes the social structures in which AI decision aids are embedded and examine how these structures shape trust in AI. The framework brings together sociological theories on how trust assessments are shaped by past experiences ( ‘shadow of the past’ ), differentiated accounts of institutional trust , and theories of trust transfer . We analyze the case of an AI-augmented geographic information system (AI-GIS) developed to support spatial planning for onshore wind energy in Germany, a field characterized by regulatory complexity and contestation. By combining qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) with qualitative content analysis, the study identifies four distinct ways in which trust in AI is socially embedded: (1) trust in decision-makers extends to AI-GIS as a tool they employ; (2) mistrust in institutions gives rise to trust in AI-GIS as a means of compensating for institutional shortcomings; (3) generalized distrust in decision-makers and institutions is transferred to AI-GIS as a continuation of existing, distrusted structures; (4) trust in institutions and distrust in decision-makers remain disconnected from mistrust in AI-GIS.

items.title: Understanding Clinician Engagement with AI in Radiology: Protocol for a Pre-Implementation Qualitative Study to Inform Learning-to-Defer System Design
items.abstract: This project is a qualitative study of clinical decision-making in chest X-ray (CXR) interpretation at Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust (OUH), a setting in which multiple AI tools have recently been evaluated and in which a Learning-to-defer (L2D) system is in development. It constitutes a case study of clinician engagement with AI in radiology. This sits within a broader project examining how cognitive mechanisms and system-level factors shape clinicians' engagement with AI tools across different stages of development, implementation, and use. At the radiology site, this work will inform the design of a prototype L2D system: a human–AI set-up in which the AI either makes a decision itself or routes (defers) it to a human, based on their respective past performance. Component A of this protocol addresses the question of how trust, advice-taking, and group decision-making operate within the CXR reporting pathway, and what sociotechnical conditions shape AI engagement in this setting. It will also explore the system attributes which influence the safe implementation of an L2D tool that is being developed for radiology. Component B of the protocol directly addresses questions related to the design requirements of the L2D system: what deferral format would clinicians accept, who should receive deferred cases, how should deferral decisions be presented, and what outcome criteria would constitute meaningful benefit? These questions require an understanding of the psychological mechanisms that clinicians rely on when engaging with AI tools, and of the clinical system in which clinicians work. Overall, the study aims to build the evidence base that responsible development and deployment of such a system will require. This way, the technical design of the L2D system can be grounded in an understanding of who makes decisions, how, under what conditions, and practically what meaningful benefit would look like in this setting. The analysis draws on theories of trust, advice-taking, and group decision-making, situated within sociotechnical frameworks for understanding healthcare work (Systems Engineering Initiative for Patient Safety [SEIPS] 2.0; nonadoption, abandonment, scale-up, spread, and sustainability [NASSS] framework).

items.title: Verification Behaviour as a Link Between Trust in Augmented Analytics and Perceived Decision Quality
items.abstract: Augmented analytics shifts much of the analytical work in business intelligence (BI) to artificial intelligence (AI), leaving non-technical users with one remaining safeguard: verifying AI-generated insights before acting on them. This paper examines whether trust in augmented analytics is associated with less verification and how verification relates to perceived decision quality. Survey data from 350 non-technical BI users in Vietnam were analysed with partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM), using a newly developed ten-item verification behaviour scale (VER). The results suggest that trust is negatively associated with verification, and verification is positively associated with perceived decision quality. The indirect association of trust through verification is negative, whereas its direct association remains positive, consistent with competitive mediation. Perceived explainability is associated with higher trust, but its direct association with verification is not significant, and the hypothesized moderating role of AI literacy receives no statistical support. Because the design is cross-sectional and self-reported, the paths represent associations rather than causal effects. Automation complacency and objective decision quality were not measured, and the verification scale was supported by initial validation evidence from one sample. The findings motivate linking insights to their source data, second checks for high-value decisions and direct monitoring of verification; the effectiveness of these proposals remains untested. The study develops a survey measure of verification behaviour with initial validation evidence and shows that the positive trust–decision quality association coexists with a negative indirect association through verification.

items.title: When Experience Becomes Metric: Systemic Model of Distress in Intelligent Digital Environments (SMDIDE)
items.abstract: The disruptions generated by AI within production systems alter the human experience at work and outline the emergence of digital distress in contemporary labor environments. The model was developed through a conceptual methodology based on interdisciplinary synthesis, integrating sociotechnical studies, cognitive psychology, labor theory, and critical AI scholarship. As a result, the SM-DIDE model conceptualizes distress as a dynamic process that arises during human-machine interaction, where cognitive and technological overload is processed as cognitive demand through the functional articulation of six interdependent subsystems. The activation, modulation, and feedback among these subsystems explain the variability in the presentation, course, and trajectories of distress. Three subsystems describe the progression from the perception of cognitive and technological demand to the emergence of evolutionary trajectories. This progression is neither linear nor deterministic: it is modulated by the transversal subsystem of involuntary regulation and by the dysfunctional coping subsystem, both of which interact with the direct influence of the structural modulation subsystem to determine the load exerted on the worker during the interaction with AI. The model reframes distress as a process and directs research toward work environments centered on human experience, integrating domains rarely articulated together—cognitive, epistemic, affective, existential, and sociotechnical—and advancing toward a unified theory of digital distress.

items.title: Where Does Accountability Lie in Deployed AI Systems? Using Cognitive Work Analysis to Address the Value-Alignment Problem
items.abstract: Increased use of Artificial Intelligence raises questions around mitigating unintended consequences. Technical perspectives on these questions lead to calls for “Responsible AI,” while regulatory perspectives lead to calls for increased human oversight. Neither perspective fully addresses the core issues surrounding accountability in the sociotechnical systems in which AI operates. Human oversight is a form of supervisory control, in which the role of the human is to monitor AI performance within defined constraints, and this requires consideration of who defines the constraints, where accountability lies when the constraints are exceeded, and how AI performance can be interpreted by human supervisors. For us, constraints correspond to system’s Values and a challenge lies in aligning system operations with these Values. We demonstrate the use of Work Domain Analysis to map purpose-related functions (i.e., activity performed in a sociotechnical system) to Values (weighted according to the functional purpose of the organization).

items.title: Work motivation in a VUCA environment: a theoretical integration of self-determination theory and the job demands-resources model
items.abstract: The article presents a theoretical analysis of employee work motivation in a VUCA environment characterised by volatility, uncertainty, complexity, and ambiguity, through the lens of Self-Determination Theory (SDT) and the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model. The study aims to substantiate an integrative conceptual model of the relationships between work environment characteristics, motivational regulation, personal resources, and organisational outcomes; the methodology combines a theoretical literature review, conceptual analysis, and cross-theoretical integration of SDT and JD-R. The analysis shows that job resources support autonomous motivation by satisfying basic psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness, whereas chronically high VUCA-related demands frustrate these needs and shift motivation toward controlled regulation or amotivation. The integrative model identifies key elements — VUCA context, job demands and resources, basic psychological needs, quality of motivational regulation, social-psychological resources, proactive job crafting, and organisational outcomes — and establishes links between them; particular attention is paid to uncertainty tolerance as a personal resource that moderates the impact of an unstable environment on motivational states. The scientific novelty lies in the systematic integration of SDT and JD-R for conditions of chronic organisational uncertainty and in establishing a theoretical correspondence between Gerchikov’s motivational typology and the SDT motivational continuum.

items.title: A Connected Architecture for U.S. Corp-to-Corp Staffing: Representation, Rate Traceability, and Workforce Operations
items.abstract: The architecture described here is targeted at the U.S. market for corp-to-corp (C2C) staffing services. Requirements, representation agreements and negotiation of the rates to be paid are frequently spread out over email threads and messaging groups. Approach. A practitioner-informed conceptual design for such recruitment is developed here from the founder’s descriptions of his current workflow, supplemented by a focused narrative discussion of recruitment accountability, explainable AI and human oversight. The design here comprises six stages. Architecture. A candidate signs the right-to-represent (RTR) agreement(s) for that candidate’s submission and the employing organization acknowledges representation of the candidate(s) by the submitting organization(s). Where a subsequent rate change is negotiated with the candidate a new signature from that candidate is required. Unreadable screenshots require human review to evaluate agreement. A mismatch between the entered hours on a timesheet and the corresponding evidence uploaded by the employee (e.g. a photo of a time card) to verify those hours will block approval and, consequently, invoice transmission until that mismatch has been corrected by the employee. Status and Limitations. All of the features described here are under current development by the founder and there are currently bugs to be fixed. As far as has been reported, the integrated workflow described here has not yet undergone a structured evaluation and the diagrams provide logical components and controls to be developed and verified as required against a variety of test cases rather than a verified deployment topology. The paper reports no measured efficiency improvements, accuracy improvements, placement improvements or fairness improvements as yet.

items.title: A Teacher's Concerns about AI in Primary School: Critical Thinking, Personal Data and the Fear of Cognitive Dependence
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is already part of pupils' everyday lives and of school life. Written from the perspective of a primary school teacher and principal, this perspective paper examines three interrelated concerns of the author herself. These concerns arose from a wish to protect her pupils and led her to study the topic for her own professional development and to help her colleagues make teaching safer and better. They concern developing critical thinking towards AI-generated answers, protecting the personal data of minors, and the fear that excessive assistance from AI will weaken pupils' thinking. Drawing on a narrative, non-systematic review of recent research on cognitive offloading, the European and Greek regulatory framework, and illustrative examples from the author's own teaching practice and lesson scenarios for primary school, it argues that the fear of cognitive dependence is a plausible concern rather than an established finding for primary school pupils. The available evidence, which comes mainly from adolescents and adults, suggests that the form of AI support (whether it replaces the learner's effort or scaffolds it) may be an important factor. AI is regarded throughout as a valuable tool; the risk lies mainly in the way it is used. The classroom examples come from ordinary lessons whose only purpose was to teach pupils to question AI answers and to protect themselves when using AI. They were not planned as research, no research data were collected, and they are offered as the author's practitioner reflections, not as findings. The author's classroom experience illustrates that such activities can be implemented in ordinary primary school lessons, but their effects on pupils' critical thinking have not yet been evaluated. The paper relates the three concerns to long-standing educational principles, in particular Socratic questioning, Dewey's reflective thought and Vygotskian scaffolding. On this basis, it proposes a simple, as yet untested three-step classroom protocol (``think -- ask -- check''), age-appropriate data protection rules, and a role for school leadership, and outlines questions for future research.

items.title: AI-enabled talent analytics and workforce agility in manufacturing SMEs: the mediating role of human-AI collaboration and the moderating role of technostress resilience
items.abstract: Introduction Small and medium-sized enterprises increasingly use AI-enabled talent analytics (AITA) to support workforce planning and adaptive performance, yet the mechanisms linking AITA to workforce agility (WA) remain underexplored. This study examines human-AI collaboration (HAIC) as a mediating mechanism and technostress resilience (TR) as a psychological resource and boundary condition. Methods A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted with 334 owners, HR managers, and operations/production heads from Pakistani manufacturing SMEs actively using AITA. Exploratory factor analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modeling, 5,000 bootstrap resamples, and moderation analyses were used to assess the measurement and structural models. Results AITA was positively associated with WA, and HAIC showed a significant indirect association between AITA and WA, consistent with partial statistical mediation. TR was positively associated with WA and significantly strengthened the AITA-WA association. The exploratory TR x HAIC interaction was not statistically significant. Discussion The findings position AITA as a socio-technical work-design resource whose association with agility depends on human interpretation, collaborative routines, and psychological capacity to manage technology-related demands. Because the data are cross-sectional and based on one knowledgeable respondent per firm, the results should be interpreted as manager-perceived associations rather than causal effects.

items.title: Algorithmic Management as a Double-Edged Form of Digital Work Design: Job Demands, Autonomy and Employee Outcomes across 35 European Countries
items.abstract: Computer-based managerial systems are part of the digital infrastructure of work, with potential implications for employee demands and discretion. Drawing on Job Demands-Resources theory, this study examines task allocation, work scheduling and performance monitoring as distinct functions and their parallel indirect associations with engagement and intention to quit through work intensity and autonomy. Weighted least squares mean- and variance-adjusted structural equation models were estimated for 26,504 employees in 35 European countries using the 2024 European Working Conditions Survey. The measures capture reported computer involvement rather than verified artificial intelligence capabilities. Engagement and autonomy were modelled as latent factors, and quit intention as an ordinal outcome. All three practices were positively associated with work intensity. Task allocation was positively associated with autonomy, whereas monitoring was negatively associated with autonomy; scheduling’s negative autonomy association was less robust to contextual fixed effects. Task allocation showed opposing indirect engagement associations through intensity and autonomy, whereas monitoring showed negative associations through both pathways. Intensity-related indirect associations with quit intention were consistently positive, while autonomy-related indirect associations were not statistically significant in the primary or fixed-effects models. Sensitivity analyses supported the main directional patterns, while exploratory country diagnostics indicated incomplete measurement invariance and heterogeneous slopes. The findings inform the evaluation of digital management by distinguishing functions associated with greater demands and greater autonomy from those associated with greater demands and reduced autonomy. The cross-sectional design does not establish causal mediation or uniform cross-country relationships.

items.title: ALGORITMA SEBAGAI REKAN KERJA: TINJAUAN SISTEMATIS TENTANG DINAMIKA TIM MANUSIA-AI DAN ANJLOKNYA KENDALI MANUSIA (LEMBAGA MANUSIA)
items.abstract: Abstrak: Kecerdasan buatan (artificial intelligence/AI) semakin terlibat dalam pekerjaan organisasi, bukan hanya sebagai alat bantu, melainkan juga sebagai rekan tim semiotonom yang berpartisipasi dalam pembagian tugas, koordinasi, dan pengambilan keputusan. Perkembangan ini menimbulkan pertanyaan tentang cara mempertahankan agensi dan kendali manusia ketika pekerjaan dilakukan bersama AI. Penelitian ini bertujuan mensintesis literatur mengenai dinamika tim manusia-AI dengan berfokus pada alokasi tugas dan otomasi, komunikasi dan kepercayaan, serta mekanisme desain yang dapat menjaga agensi manusia. Penelitian menggunakan metode tinjauan pustaka sistematis (systematic literature review/SLR) dengan proses seleksi berorientasi PRISMA.Tinjauan melaporkan 13 studi yang memenuhi kriteria, terbit pada 2023-2026, dengan desain yang beragam, meliputi tinjauan konseptual, tinjauan integratif dan sistematis, eksperimen, metode campuran, analisis teks, serta studi kasus industri. Sintesis naratif disusun dalam tiga tema, yaitu AI sebagai rekan kerja, dinamika tim manusia-AI, serta erosi agensi dan pengawasan manusia. Berdasarkan ringkasan studi ,alokasi tugas dinamis, antarmuka yang transparan dan dapat dijelaskan, kewenangan intervensi manusia, verifikasi aktif, dan model mental bersama berpotensi mendukung kendali manusia. Sebaliknya, otomasi tinggi tanpa keterlibatan manusia yang memadai, pengawasan pasif, dan ketergantungan tanpa evaluasi kritis dapat melemahkan kesadaran situasional, otonomi, dan akuntabilitas. Temuan ini mengindikasikan bahwa organisasi perlu merancang pekerjaan berbasis AI dengan kepercayaan yang terkalibrasi, tanggung jawab yang jelas, dan peluang intervensi manusia yang bermakna. Keterbatasan draf terkait jumlah hasil penyaringan dan penilaian risiko bias formal perlu diverifikasi sebelum publikasi.

items.title: Assessing learning beyond AI assistance: assisted performance and unaided retention in generative AI-supported learning
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can improve task performance when support is available, yet these gains do not necessarily indicate what learners retain independently. This Mini Review examines three assessment conditions: assisted task performance, immediate testing without AI, and delayed testing without AI. Relevant evidence was identified through searches of the Web of Science Core Collection and supplementary source identification. Across the reviewed experiments, outcomes varied with task demands, instructional design and the skills assessed. Unrestricted AI assistance was associated with weaker subsequent performance in some comparisons, whereas structured AI-supported instruction showed benefits for selected outcomes. None of the twelve selected studies documented all three conditions with verified AI exclusion at both no-AI posttests. Variation in baseline measurement, follow-up intervals and instructional comparators further limits cross-study interpretation. Retrieval attempts, elaboration and feedback use offer plausible explanations, but their roles as mediators remain largely untested. Future studies should document AI availability during learning and testing, specify the constructs assessed, and report learning activities between assessments.

items.title: Associations Between Perceived Generative AI Support Features and Self-Reported Deep Knowledge Construction Among Chinese University Students
items.abstract: As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in higher education, a central sustainability challenge is whether greater access to AI support can be achieved without weakening the learner’s self-regulation required for meaningful knowledge construction. Yet it remains unclear which forms of perceived AI support are associated with deeper knowledge construction and through which learner-level regulatory pathways this association operates. This study examines six perceived support features—fine-grainedness (FG), transparency in reasoning (TR), adaptivity in explanation (AE), strategy instruction embeddedness (SIE), multimodal richness (MR), and social presence (SP)—and their associations with self-reported deep knowledge construction (DKC). Survey data from 626 Chinese university students were analysed using covariance-based structural equation modelling, latent-variable bootstrap analysis, and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis. FG, TR, and AE showed significant direct associations with DKC, whereas SIE, MR, and SP did not. Ten of 12 hypothesised indirect associations involving self-efficacy (SE) and metacognitive monitoring (MM) were supported; the AE → MM → DKC and MR → MM → DKC pathways were not. Two configurations were associated with high DKC, with TR and AE recurring as core conditions. Given the cross-sectional, self-reported design, these findings indicate associations rather than causal effects or direct sustainability outcomes. They inform the educationally sustainable integration of generative AI by identifying learner-regulatory processes associated with knowledge construction.
